title: YOU ARE NOT YOUR OWN: The Verse We Quote Like Comfort—Until We Realize What Jesus Actually Bought
paragraphs: YOU ARE NOT YOUR OWN: The Verse We Quote Like Comfort—Until We Realize What Jesus Actually Bought

What if the words “you are not your own” were never meant to crush your identity—but to expose the lie that has been quietly destroying it? Paul’s words are more confronting, more beautiful, and far more costly than they first appear.
There is a sentence in the Bible that our generation may find almost offensive.
Not because it is cruel.
Because it reaches into the one place we desperately want to keep locked.
The place marked:
Mine.
My body.
My desires.
My sexuality.
My money.
My ambitions.
My future.
My private habits.
My pain.
My decisions.
My life.
We may give Jesus Sunday morning.
We may give Him worship songs, prayers before meals, Bible verses in our social media bios, and tears when life becomes unbearable.
But somewhere beneath all of that can remain one final locked room.
The room where we quietly whisper:
“Jesus, You can have everything else.
But this is mine.”
Then the apostle Paul walks directly toward that locked door.
And he writes words that leave almost no room for negotiation:
οὐκ ἐστὲ ἑαυτῶν
ouk este heautōn.
Literally:
“You are not your own.”
And suddenly Christianity becomes much more than inspiration.
Much more than self-improvement.
Much more than adding Jesus to the life we already planned to live.
Because the Gospel does not merely announce that Jesus wants to improve your life.
It announces that Jesus Christ died and rose again—and that the person who belongs to Him has been redeemed at a price.
Maybe that makes something inside you uncomfortable.
Good.
Stay here.
Because if you leave too quickly, you may hear only the demand and miss the breathtaking reason behind it.
Paul did not write “you are not your own” into a vacuum.
The words appear in 1 Corinthians 6:19–20, and their context matters enormously.
Corinth was a complicated city, and the Corinthian church was a complicated church.
These were not polished saints floating three inches above the ground.
They were people being pulled out of old identities, old sexual patterns, old philosophies, old loyalties, old wounds, and old ways of understanding freedom.
Paul had just confronted sexual immorality.
And then he said something astonishing about the Christian body.
He asked whether they knew that their body was a temple of the Holy Spirit within them, whom they had from God.
Then came the words:
καὶ οὐκ ἐστὲ ἑαυτῶν· ἠγοράσθητε γὰρ τιμῆς.
καὶ οὐκ ἐστὲ ἑαυτῶν — “and you are not your own.”
ἠγοράσθητε γὰρ τιμῆς — “for you were bought with a price.”
The verb ἠγοράσθητε — ēgorasthēte comes from agorazō, a word meaning to buy or purchase.
Paul's point is not that Christians are worthless possessions.
It is almost the opposite.
There was a price.
And Scripture does not leave us guessing about what redemption ultimately cost.
Peter writes that believers were redeemed not with perishable things such as silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ, “like that of a lamb without blemish or spot” (1 Peter 1:18–19).
Jesus Himself said that the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve and to give His life as a ransom for many (Mark 10:45).
Revelation celebrates the Lamb because He was slain and by His blood ransomed people for God from every tribe, language, people, and nation (Revelation 5:9).
So when Paul says,
“You are not your own,”
he is not introducing religious tyranny.
He is pointing toward Calvary.
You were bought.
But look carefully at the Buyer.
His hands are pierced.
The One claiming you is the One who gave Himself for you.
That changes everything.
Because Jesus did not stand at a safe distance from your ruin and demand that you climb your way back to Him.
He entered human history.
He took flesh.
He walked among sinners.
He touched the unclean.
He welcomed the rejected.
He confronted hypocrites.
He ate with people whose reputations made religious crowds uncomfortable.
Then, though He was without sin, He went to a Roman cross.
Betrayed.
Mocked.
Beaten.
Crucified.
And there the sinless Son of God bore sin.
Not because sin was insignificant.
Because it was so devastating that redemption would cost blood.
The Gospel does not say:
“Your sin doesn't matter.”
The Gospel says:
“Your sin mattered enough for Christ to die—and His grace is powerful enough to forgive the sinner who comes to Him.”
That is why “you are not your own” is terrifying to the ego...
and beautiful to the exhausted soul.
Because being your own god is exhausting.
You have to define yourself.
Save yourself.
Validate yourself.
Protect yourself.
Justify yourself.
Invent your purpose.
Carry your shame.
Repair your past.
Control your future.
And when everything collapses, you have nobody greater than yourself to fall upon.
The modern promise of absolute autonomy sounds like freedom:
“It's your life.”
“Follow your heart.”
“Do whatever makes you happy.”
“Nobody can tell you what to do with your body.”
But Scripture asks a deeper question:
What happens when the heart you are following is wounded?
What happens when the desire you are obeying becomes your master?
What happens when what made you happy for ten minutes leaves you empty for ten years?
What happens when “my truth” cannot wash away actual guilt?
What happens when the freedom you demanded quietly becomes the chain you cannot break?
Jesus said that everyone who practices sin is a slave to sin, but if the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed (John 8:34–36).
Biblical freedom, then, is not simply the ability to do whatever desire demands.
It is freedom from sin so that we can belong to God.
That is the scandal.
And that is the grace.
Maybe this is where the article stops being about “people” and starts becoming about you.
Because there may be something you call private that Jesus calls His.
The browser history nobody sees.
The relationship you know is pulling you away from God.
The bitterness you have rehearsed so many times that it now feels like part of your personality.
The secret sexual compromise.
The addiction you keep renaming as stress relief.
The money you cannot surrender.
The applause you need.
The resentment you protect.
The person you refuse to forgive.
The ambition that matters more to you than obedience.
The hidden conversation.
The second account.
The secret life.
The carefully managed Christian appearance covering a soul that is becoming exhausted from pretending.
And perhaps you have learned how to say all the right things.
“God knows my heart.”
Yes.
That should comfort us.
And sometimes it should terrify us.
Because God knows the heart beneath the performance too.
He knows what nobody else knows.
He knows what you deleted.
He knows what you almost did.
He knows why you really went back.
He knows what you secretly want.
He knows the prayer you stopped praying because you were afraid obedience might be the answer.
Yet here is where Christianity becomes unlike mere moralism.
Jesus does not expose sinners simply to humiliate them.
He exposes darkness in order to bring people into light.
The same Christ who says “repent” is the Christ whose blood provides forgiveness.
The same Gospel that destroys our excuses destroys our hopelessness.
Paul had already reminded these Corinthians what some of them had once been.
His list in 1 Corinthians 6 is uncomfortable.
Sexual sinners.
Idolaters.
Adulterers.
Thieves.
The greedy.
Drunkards.
Reviling people.
Swindlers.
Then comes one of the most beautiful turns in the entire passage:
καὶ ταῦτά τινες ἦτε
“And such were some of you.”
Were.
That word carries thunder.
Not because Christians become instantly flawless.
Not because temptation disappears.
Not because every consequence of yesterday vanishes overnight.
But because grace means your sin no longer has the authority to write the final sentence of your identity.
Paul continues: they had been washed, sanctified, and justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of God (1 Corinthians 6:11).
Do you see it?
The Bible does not pretend the scandal never happened.
It announces that scandal does not have to have the last word.
You sinned.
But Christ saves sinners.
You wandered.
But the Shepherd still calls wandering sheep home.
You fell.
But grace can meet you on the ground.
You compromised.
But repentance is still possible.
You became someone you once promised yourself you would never become.
But Jesus Christ is still Jesus Christ.
This is not permission to continue sinning.
Grace is not God's way of helping us become comfortable with rebellion.
Paul demolishes that distortion in Romans 6.
If we have been united with Christ, we are not called to make peace with the slavery from which He came to deliver us.
Grace forgives.
Grace also transforms.
Grace receives you as you come.
And grace loves you too much to enthrone the chains that are killing you.
That is why “you are not your own” eventually becomes one of the safest truths a believer can hear.
Your body belongs to Christ.
Your sexuality belongs to Christ.
Your singleness belongs to Christ.
Your marriage belongs to Christ.
Your career belongs to Christ.
Your influence belongs to Christ.
Your possessions belong under Christ's lordship.
Your plans belong under Christ's lordship.
Your wounds belong in Christ's hands.
Your future belongs to Christ.
Even your suffering is not meaningless territory abandoned by God.
You belong to Jesus.
Paul therefore ends the thought with an imperative:
δοξάσατε δὴ τὸν θεὸν ἐν τῷ σώματι ὑμῶν.
Doxasate dē ton Theon en tō sōmati hymōn.
In straightforward English:
“Therefore glorify God in your body.”
Notice the movement.
You are not your own.
You were bought with a price.
Therefore glorify God.
Grace comes before the command.
Redemption comes before the response.
Christ's purchase becomes the foundation of Christian surrender.
We do not surrender ourselves to make Jesus love us.
We surrender because in Christ we have encountered a love so costly that keeping the throne for ourselves no longer makes sense.
This matters because Christianity can easily become another performance.
Read more.
Pray harder.
Serve more.
Give more.
Share more.
Do more.
And perhaps, somewhere underneath it, we begin trying to purchase what Christ already purchased for us.
But you cannot buy the blood of Jesus.
You cannot donate your way into forgiveness.
You cannot share enough Christian articles to erase your sins.
You cannot purchase salvation from Gospel Warrior or from any ministry on earth.
Salvation is by God's grace, received through faith in Jesus Christ, not something we earn through works (Ephesians 2:8–9).
That distinction matters.
Supporting Gospel work can be an act of stewardship and worship when it comes from faith, love, generosity, and a desire to help truth reach others.
But Jesus Christ alone saves.
So if this article has confronted you, do not merely support a page.
Surrender to the Savior.
Maybe your prayer tonight does not need impressive vocabulary.
Maybe it sounds more like:
“Jesus... I have been calling mine what belongs to You.”
Maybe:
“Lord, forgive me.”
Maybe:
“I don't know how to get free, but I know I need You.”
Maybe:
“No more hiding.”
That may be where repentance begins.
Not with pretending you were never dirty.
But with finally walking into the light because you believe Jesus is better than the darkness you have been protecting.
And if this exposed something you have kept hidden, you do not need to tell strangers every detail. But you can refuse to keep pretending.
Not as a performance.
Not as an algorithmic ritual.
As an honest confession that somebody else reading in silence may desperately need to see.
Because somewhere on your Facebook friends list is probably someone who would never search for a sermon.
They may never walk into a church this week.
But they trust you.
And your share may put the truth in front of them at the exact moment their private world is collapsing.
Send it privately to the believer who has drifted.
Send it to the person who thinks their past has permanently disqualified them from grace.
Send it even to the skeptical friend who believes Christianity is only about religious people pretending to be good.
Let them discover what the Gospel actually says:
We were not good enough.
Christ was.
We could not redeem ourselves.
Christ came for sinners.
And resurrection means the cross was not the end.

If you want to glorify God with what He has entrusted to you, supporting faithful Gospel work can be one practical expression of that stewardship—but never confuse supporting a ministry with earning God's favor.
If Gospel Warrior is helping you know Christ, understand Scripture, repent honestly, heal biblically, and grow deeper in discipleship, then consider staying close to this mission.
Jesus is not asking you to become a customer.
He calls sinners to become disciples.
He is not offering merchandise in exchange for redemption.
He offers Himself.
The cross cannot be purchased.
Grace cannot be merchandised.
Forgiveness cannot be earned.
Christ paid the price.
And because He paid it, Christianity asks the question we spend much of our lives avoiding:
If Jesus really died for me...
if He really rose...
if my body really belongs to Him...
if my life really belongs under His lordship...
then what am I still refusing to surrender?
Read that again.
Slowly.
What are you still calling mine that Jesus is asking you to place into His hands?
Maybe that question hurts.
Let it.
Not every pain is destruction.
Sometimes conviction is the mercy of God refusing to let us comfortably destroy ourselves.
The answer is not self-hatred.
The answer is not religious shame.
The answer is not trying harder until God finally tolerates you.
The answer is Christ.
Repentance toward God.
Faith in Jesus Christ.
The mercy purchased at the cross.
The transforming presence of the Holy Spirit.
A new allegiance.
A new Master.
A new direction.
A life increasingly able to say:
“My body is Yours.”
“My future is Yours.”
“My sexuality is Yours.”
“My money is Yours.”
“My ambitions are Yours.”
“My wounds are Yours.”
“My secret places are Yours.”
“My reputation is Yours.”
“My plans are Yours.”
“My life is Yours.”
“Jesus...
I am Yours.”
That is the truth behind “you are not your own.”
It is not the announcement that you have become worthless.
It is the announcement that you have been redeemed.
Not abandoned.
Bought at a price.
Not free to return peacefully to the chains from which Christ came to rescue you.
Free to glorify the One who loved you unto death.
So when temptation whispers, “My body, my choice,” remember whose blood bought you.
When shame whispers, “Your past owns you,” remember whose blood bought you.
When culture whispers, “Invent yourself,” remember whose name is now over you.
When Satan accuses, when old desires return, when yesterday comes knocking, when you stumble and wonder whether grace could possibly still reach someone like you...
look again toward the cross.
The scars of Jesus say your sin was serious.
The empty tomb says your sin does not have to win.
And the Gospel says that when a sinner comes to Christ, the darkest chapter does not get to name the book.
The world may remember your scandal. Jesus can still write your redemption.
